references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same parable about children sitting in the marketplace calling to each other, saying they played the flute but no one danced, and mourned but no one wept. The wording is almost identical.

The proverb speaks of how, regardless of what a wise man does toward a fool—whether he is angry or laughs—he finds no rest. This reflects the theme in Luke 7:32 that people do not respond regardless of the approach used.
Isaiah speaks of God giving the people rest, but they would not listen. This illustrates the same pattern of rejecting God's message no matter how it is presented.
Lamentations describes sorrow and weeping, which corresponds to the image of singing laments while no one weeps—an image of rejecting the message of repentance.

The following verses in Luke explain the parable: John came fasting (lament), and they called him possessed; the Son of Man came eating and drinking (flute-playing/joy), and they called him a glutton. Wisdom is justified by her children.
A similar theme of rejection: The religious leaders refused to answer whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men, thereby rejecting both John's and Jesus' authority.

Ezekiel describes the people coming and hearing God's word as a beautiful song, but not acting on it. They hear the words but do nothing—an image parallel to children who respond neither to flute-playing nor to lament.
